messages.subject: Re: QTL analysis with quantitative covariate
messages.body_plain:
Dear Prof. Karl

The case that you mentioned " if the effects are Q -> X -> Y, where Q is the QTL, X is the covariate, and Y is the phenotype, then you'll eliminate the QTL effect by conditioning on X ", is the case of an interactive covariate?

Best Regards,
Farah

On Friday, April 18, 2014 2:30:54 PM UTC+8, Farah GG wrote:
> Dear Prof. Karl,
>
> Now, I want to add a quantitative covariate (proline content) to my qtl analysis. Anova and boxplot show that it is a additive covariate, as expected. But, I do not know what is wrong in my command entering that after adding the covariate, my main qtl (LOD:22.3) declined, and now it is not significant.
> Would you please clarify it for me? Thank you very much.
> Regards,
> Farah,
>
> If the covariate is highly correlated with the primary phenotype, you may be eliminating the QTL effect by conditioning on it.
> That is, if the effects are Q -> X -> Y, where Q is the QTL, X is the covariate, and Y is the phenotype, then you'll eliminate the QTL effect by conditioning on X.
>
> See chapter 7 of the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book).
>
>
> Ok. Thanks Prof. In this case, I can not add effect of covariate in the qtl analysis?
>
> Best,
> Farah,
>

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL analysis with quantitative covariate
messages.body_plain:
Dear Prof. Karl,

Thank you very much. But, when Pearson’s correlation between my phenotype and covariate (proline) is 0.61 at the 0.01 level, how I can find whether my covariate is additive or interactive?
I did Anova:

Analysis of Variance Table

              Df     Sum Sq       Mean Sq      F value           Pr(>F)

proline     1     265973         265973        109.78           < 2.2e-16 ***

Residuals 187 453078    2423

***************************************************************************

I also did makeqtl & fitqtl in this way (out<- scanone(alico2, addcovar=covar,method="hk") :

Drop one QTL at a time ANOVA table:

----------------------------------

                df       Type III SS         LOD            %var           F value            Pvalue(Chi2)          Pvalue(F)

4...@34.5     2       42733               4.864            5.682          11.58                  0                      1.84e-05 ***

8...@68.2     2      259983             23.330           34.571          70.43                 0                      < 2e-16 ***

**************************************************************************

Estimated effects:

-----------------

                  est         SE            t

Intercept    65.131     3.148      20.689

4...@34.5a   24.935     5.226      4.771

4...@34.5d   -5.367      6.530     -0.822

8...@68.2a    54.129    4.616     11.726

8...@68.2d   -13.488    6.405     -2.106

Would you please clarify me that based on my results my covariate is additive or interactive?

Thank you so much, in advance.

Best Regards,

Farah

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL analysis with quantitative covariate
messages.body_plain:
The question is then whether there is a QTL x covariate interaction, which you could investigate by fitting the model with the covariate as strictly additive and then as interactive, and taking the difference in LOD scores; if large, that indicates that there is evidence for a QTL x covariate interaction.

I would also look at a scatterplot of the phenotype and the covariate, with points colored by there QTL genotype.

karl

messages.subject: Flip map (invert marker order of a whole linkage group/chromosome)
messages.subject_clean: Flip map (invert marker order of a whole linkage group/chromosome)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

is there a function to flip the complete map order of a linkage group/chromosome? I searched the manuals but could not find something like that (or I overlooked it).
This might be useful, if the map order obtained is inverted compared to a reference map or maps from other studies.
I know this can be done "by hand", but I would find this very helpful in the package and if it is not too much work, this might be an idea for a future update.

Just to make clear what I mean:
Marker order obtained by mapping: (top) M4-M3-M2-M1 (bottom)
Marker order reference map: (top / short arm) M1-M2-M3-M4 (bottom / long arm)

Best regards,
Eva

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Flip map (invert marker order of a whole linkage group/chromosome)
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Flip map (invert marker order of a whole linkage group/chromosome)
messages.body_plain:
You can use switch.order. For example:

  hyper <- switch.order(hyper, chr=4, nmar(hyper)[4]:1)

It does seem a good idea to have an invert.order function. Sort of like this:

  invert.order <- function(cross, chr, ...) switch.order(cross, chr, nmar(cross)[chr]:1, ...)

karl

messages.body_plain:
It's hard to tell without further information.

For the first error, could you send me the data privately, and I'll try to see what's going on?

For the second error, you're running out of memory; you either need a machine with more RAM, or try using a smaller number for the "window" argument. For example:

   data <- orderMarkers(data, chr=2, use.ripple=TRUE, window=4, error.prob=0.003, map.function="kosambi")

karl

messages.body_plain:
The first error is caused by you having multiple markers with the same name. Each marker name needs to be unique.

I fixed this by just omitting the second instance of each marker:

  mn <- markernames(data, chr=1)
  tab <- table(mn)
  dup_names <- names(tab)[tab > 1]
  col2drop <- NULL
  for(i in dup_names)
      col2drop <- c(col2drop, which(mn==i)[-1])
  data$geno[[1]]$data <- data$geno[[1]]$data[,-col2drop]
  data$geno[[1]]$map <- data$geno[[1]]$map[-col2drop]

karl

messages.subject: Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
messages.subject_clean: Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl et al,
I am working with expression phenotypes- lots of them (>20,000).
For many of these, the appropriate model is 2part, because there are many 0 counts. I am trying apply the same pipeline to all phenotypes - 10k scantwo perms, stepwise model selection, output various stats. So, instead of running 2part, which cannot be fit in scantwo/stepwiseQTL, I am planning on running two rounds, one normal (excluding the 0 count phenotypes) and one binary (all 0-counts set to 0 and all others set to 1).

Here's the problem: scantwo perms for model = "binary" is extremely slow. So slow that it is not feasible to run on a 24 cluster 48gb node on our server, even for a single phenotype, let alone 20,000. The other analyses are relatively fast, even with model = binary. So, I am looking for a way around running the scantwo permutations.

Here's my thought process: For binary traits, there should be some global permutation levels that apply to all traits, no matter the study (right?). Kind of like taking a single set of permutations for a dataset of quantile normalized phenotypes. If that is the case, the n(0)/n(1) for a given binary phenotype should always return a single, exact permutation threshold. Therefore we could predict the permutation thresholds for any binary phenotype by the ratio of 0's:1's using a non-linear (or linear) regression.

Solutions?:
1) Is there an easy way to speed up the model = "binary" scantwos? I imagine not, but if so, great!
2) If not, what if we got our hands on a huge node >= 1tb and ran 10k perms for 10 sets of binary phenotypes with 0/1 ratios of .05, .1, .15, .20, .25, .30, .35, .40, .45, .50. Would it be statistically sound to then fit a model and predict the thresholds at all 0/1 ratios and use those for each gene expression phenotype? If so, we could then get around running 20k sets of perms with just 10.
Thoughts?
Thanks for all of the help!
John

John T. Lovell, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Fellow
Department of Integrative Biology
University of Texas, Austin

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
messages.body_plain:
The binary trait analysis is slower than that for a regular quantitative trait because it uses an iterative algorithm to fit a logistic regression model. So at each pair of locations, a series of regressions will be fit, instead of just one.

I like your solution (2). You might want to use more ratios at the low end than the high end...perhaps something like 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5.

You might also play with reducing the number of iterations in the fit. You might even want to go into the C code and change the stopping rule. (I'm thinking that, for the purpose of permutations, one would want to stop early if the LOD score is not big, and go longer only if there's evidence that the LOD score is going to be largish.)

Regards,
karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] scantwo permutation took too long
messages.body_plain:
Scantwo permutations take a long time, especially if you have many markers.

1000 permutations will take at least as 1000x as long as running scantwo once, and there can problems with running out of memory which will really slow things down.

If you can use method="hk", things will be much faster.

Also try the scantwopermhk() function, which works only for Haley-Knott regression, but was reorganized to try to speed things up.

I'd also recommend doing the permutations in smaller batches and then combining the results with c().

karl

messages.body_plain:
John,

It might be due to low counts when you cross-tabulate the binary phenotype with all the QTL in your model.  This happens in logistic regression if you have too many variables in your model or if they are collinear or if the binary phenotype is has low frequency.

- Decrease the number of QTL you consider
- Decrease number of linked or interacting QTL

Failing these, add a small amount of noise (with variance 0.01) to the phenotype and treat the data as normal.

Other solutions to consider would involve tacking the numerical algorithm directly.

Saunak

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Saunak!
I think you are right; I typically am getting errors from samples that have only a few observations in one cell of the test. Not sure how I'll be able to get around that in my current experimental design while using model = "binary".
So, have you explored the performance of adding variance to binary traits and fitting them as normal? If this approach is robust, it could dramatically speed up my pipeline. Here is a comparison of the binary model and the normal model, fit to the data with sd = 0.01 around 0 or 1 for the 1st 5 of my binary traits:
https://johntlovell.files.wordpress.com/2014/10/binary-normal-comps.pdf
Basically, when the binary model converges, we get nearly identical scanone profiles, with the normal model fitting slightly better. When the binary model does not converge, we get much better fits from the normal model.
Thoughts?
John

On Friday, January 30, 2015 at 11:57:07 AM UTC-6, Saunak Sen wrote:
> John,
>
> It might be due to low counts when you cross-tabulate the binary phenotype with all the QTL in your model.  This happens in logistic regression if you have too many variables in your model or if they are collinear or if the binary phenotype is has low frequency.
>
> - Decrease the number of QTL you consider
> - Decrease number of linked or interacting QTL
>
> Failing these, add a small amount of noise (with variance 0.01) to the phenotype and treat the data as normal.
>
> Other solutions to consider would involve tacking the numerical algorithm directly.
>
> Saunak
>
> On Thursday, January 29, 2015 at 10:16:29 AM UTC-8, John Lovell wrote:
> > Hi Karl,
> > Thanks for the response.
> > I am working on implementing model = "binary" in my QTL pipeline and am running into some issues with convergence.
> > I sometimes receive an error from stepwiseqtl:
> > "In fitqtlengine(pheno = pheno, qtl = qtl, covar = covar, formula = formula,  : Didn't converge."

> >
> > Do you have any thoughts on what might be constraining the convergence and how I can increase the probability of convergence without increasing the tolerance?
> > Thanks,
> > John

> > On Tuesday, January 27, 2015 at 9:38:03 PM UTC-6, Karl Broman wrote:
> > > The binary trait analysis is slower than that for a regular quantitative trait because it uses an iterative algorithm to fit a logistic regression model. So at each pair of locations, a series of regressions will be fit, instead of just one.
> > >
> > > I like your solution (2). You might want to use more ratios at the low end than the high end...perhaps something like 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5.
> > >

(I'm thinking that, for the purpose of permutations, one would want to stop early if the LOD score is not big, and go longer only if there's evidence that the LOD score is going to be largish.)
